#+title: The hard part of the flying Roadster is the controller
#+author: Adolfo De Unánue
#+date: 2026-10-19
#+description: I measured Tesla's Roadster half loop and kickflip from the livestream telemetry, worked out the forces, the energy and the nitrogen, and wrote a PID controller that flies both stunts. Then I tried to break it.

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@In October 2026 Tesla showed a Roadster that drives up a curved wall until it hangs upside down, drops off the top, turns upright in the air and lands on cold-gas thrusters.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p1" data-s="1">@@Later in the same show it jumped a row of parked vehicles and rolled a full turn on the way over.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p1" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The press repeated three numbers: a 1.7-tonne car, a 600-litre tank, and nitrogen at 10 000 psi[fn:: One psi is one pound-force per square inch, 6 894.76 Pa. Ten thousand psi is 68.9 MPa; one atmosphere is 101 325 Pa, or 14.7 psi.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p1" data-s="3">@@My first reaction, on a whiteboard, was to try to show that those numbers could not work.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p1" data-s="4" data-ev>@@They can, and the reasons are in the first half of this post.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p2" data-s="0">@@The second half is about the part the numbers leave out.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Lifting two tonnes with compressed gas for a few seconds is ordinary physics.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Keeping those two tonnes on a planned path while they turn upside down, with thrusters that can only push, valves that open late, a tank that cools as it empties, and a sensor that never quite agrees with itself, is a control problem.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S0.p2" data-s="3" data-ev>@@I build the simplest controller that flies both stunts, a PID loop, check it against the telemetry, and then show where it stops being enough.@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<figure class="rf rf-pan"><div class="rf-scroll" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="My whiteboard, stitched from a phone video, scrolls sideways"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="My whiteboard, stitched from a phone video" loading="lazy"></div><figcaption>My whiteboard, stitched from a phone video; scroll sideways to read it. From left to right: the state and error vectors with the thrusters, a sketch of nitrogen's phase diagram, the jump and the forces on the car, the half loop, the PID sketch this post grew from, and my first estimate of the nitrogen. That estimate has one slip: I wrote 600 L as 600 m³, a factor of a thousand, so a density of 535 kg/m³ (the equation of state gives 495) turned 297 kg of nitrogen into about 320 tonnes. The 5 tonnes I read off the half loop was the downforce gauge, 4 698 kg of suction, about twice the car's weight. To keep the arithmetic in my head I rounded one atmosphere to 10 psi.</figcaption></figure>
#+end_export

* Tesla's demonstration and claims

#+begin_export html
<figure class="rf"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="The Roadster upside down at the top of the curved wall, with the broadcast gauges" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The car parked upside down at the top of the wall, held by its fans. The broadcast gauges read 4 698 kg of downforce, a pitch of 170° and an altitude of 68.1 ft. Frame from <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TWHXrLzUKJc&amp;t=84s">CNET's cut of the livestream</a> at 1:24.</figcaption></figure>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Tesla's livestream [cite:@tesla2026roadster] carried four demonstrations, and Tesla posted two of them as short videos [cite:@tesla2026ramp; @tesla2026kickflip].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@In the first, the car climbed a curved wall slowly, parked upside down at the top, came back down, and then repeated the climb at speed, left the top of the wall upside down and landed on its thrusters.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p1" data-s="2" data-ev>@@In the second, the car launched itself over a Tesla Semi and a row of cars, rolled through a full turn in the air and landed.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p1" data-s="3">@@The third was a 0 to 60 mph run in 0.81 seconds.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p1" data-s="4">@@In the fourth, at the end of the livestream, the car rose beside a pylon, turned over in the air and landed on its thrusters.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p1" data-s="5" data-ev>@@CNET's cut of the livestream, which I measured, ends before it, and I analyse neither of the last two.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="0">@@The people on stage made the claims that matter for this post.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@A presenter described "a fan suction system on the bottom of the car that can pull up to 2 Gs", adding that "we borrowed some technology from SpaceX to do the rest".@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="2">@@Elon Musk said the car has "attitude control thrusters and main thrusters in the rear" and "an advanced ultra-high pressure air tank" that the car recharges itself.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="3" data-ev>@@Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering, said the car carries two carbon-overwrapped tanks, "a total of 600 L", feeding ten nozzles, and a presenter said the four rear thrusters, the ones that push the car forward, create "over 80 kN of thrust".@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="4" data-ev>@@In an interview with Hagerty, recorded the day before and published the same day [cite:@hagerty2026roadster], Moravy put the car at "just under 1,700 kilos" and the tanks at 10 000 psi of nitrogen[fn:: On the livestream Moravy also put the gas at "about 250 kilos of air". At 20 °C, 250 kg in 600 litres is 6,338 psi of air or 7,143 psi of nitrogen, short of the 10 000 psi rating. I use the rating, which puts 297 kg of nitrogen in the tanks. With 250 kg every gas budget below shrinks by about a sixth, and a full tank is still one stunt.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="5">@@Those are the numbers the press repeated.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="6" data-ev>@@He also named the ten nozzles: four in the rear for the 0 to 60 run, and a flight system of "one in each corner and then two at the front to yaw".@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="7">@@Tesla said air on stage and nitrogen to Hagerty.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S1.p2" data-s="8">@@Air is 78% nitrogen by volume, and a tank of air holds about 7% more mass than the same tank of nitrogen, so I work with nitrogen and give the air figure where it matters.@@html:</span>@@

Downward plumes from the corner thrusters lift the car past the parked line. <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5vsHHPVhJg&amp;t=13s">Tesla's Kickflip video</a> at 0:13.</figcaption></figure>

* The livestream telemetry

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The broadcast overlaid the car's telemetry on the video: a left gauge that reads downforce in kilograms during the slow climb and G-force during the flights[fn:: An accelerometer cannot feel gravity. In free fall it reads zero; standing on the ground it reads 1 g, because the road pushes up. What it measures is specific force: every force except gravity, divided by the mass. In the air that is thrust and a little drag.], a pitch gauge during the climb, an altitude gauge in feet, a small 3-D model of the car that turns with the car's attitude[fn:: Attitude is the car's orientation in space, given by three angles: roll about its long axis, pitch about its side-to-side axis and yaw about its vertical axis.], and a top view of the car with six rings that light up when a thruster fires: one at each corner and two at the nose.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@I downloaded CNET's ten-minute cut of the livestream [cite:@cnet2026roadster], 1280×720 at 29.97 frames per second, and read these gauges from every frame of the three windows that matter, 14 seconds of slow climb and two flights of about five seconds each.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Off-the-shelf OCR failed on the gauges.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The HUD font draws zero with a slash, and Tesseract [cite:@smith2007tesseract] reads it as a two, so 0.9 g came back as 2.9 g.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@I segmented each gauge into glyphs, grouped 4 841 glyphs into 24 clusters, labelled the clusters once by eye, and classified every frame against them.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p2" data-s="3">@@The lamps needed no OCR: a ring reads about 55 on a 0–255 scale when dark and 165 to 190 when lit.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p2" data-s="4">@@The attitude icon I read by eye at 0.1-second steps; it is sharp at the states that are hard to confuse (upright, on a side, upside down) and good to about 20° in between.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p3" data-s="0">@@The video frames supplied the rest.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The wall's height, 21.1 m from the altitude gauge, served as a ruler for the car, which measures 4.4 m long to within half a metre once I allow for perspective.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The horizontal motion could not be measured: there is one camera, it looks at the wall at an angle, and when I scaled the car's position by the wall its height came out up to 5 m off the gauge.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p3" data-s="3" data-ev>@@I report the vertical motion from the gauges and treat the horizontal motion as a rough few metres per second.@@html:</span>@@

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---+---+---|
| Wall profile | two arcs, 9.1 m and 9.8 m radius | pitch against altitude, fit RMS 0.17 m |
| Top of the wall | 21.1 m | altitude gauge |
| Downforce at the top | 4 698 kgf | downforce gauge, car upside down |
| Slow climb | 2.0 m/s on average | pitch, altitude and the wall profile |
| Kickflip apex | 8.0 m | altitude gauge |
| Kickflip coast | 7.7 m/s² downward, so 0.22 g of lift left on | parabola fit; the gauge reads 0.2 g |
| Peak specific force | 3.2 g at the kickflip's lift-off, 2.5 g in the air; 3.3 g braking off the wall | G-force gauge |
| Thrust impulse per kg of car | 3.4 g·s kickflip, 4.6 g·s half loop | G-force gauge, integrated while airborne |
| Roll during the kickflip | 360° in 2.1 s, at rest at both ends | attitude icon, fit RMS 7° |
| Turn upright off the wall | 170° in 1.5 s | attitude icon, fit RMS 1° |
| Car length | 4.4 ± 0.5 m | video frames, wall as ruler |

On the wall the car climbs to about 21 m in 5 seconds, with no thruster lit: the fans and the tyres do that work. The right corners light just before it leaves the top upside down; it turns upright while it falls, and brakes at up to 3.3 g before a slow final descent.</figcaption></figure>

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@None of this measures the car's mass.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="1">@@Every kinematic equation divides it out, so a video can tell you accelerations and never kilograms.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="2">@@The mass needs a known force.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The broadcast offers one, and only through an assumption: the gauge read 4 700 kgf of downforce[fn:: The gauge's kilograms are kilograms-force, the weight of that many kilograms: 1 kgf is 9.81 N, so 4 700 kgf is 46.1 kN. The altitude gauge is in feet: 1 ft is 0.3048 m, so 69 ft is 21.0 m.] with the car parked at the top, and the presenter said the fans "can pull up to 2 Gs".@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="4" data-ev>@@If the fans were pulling their stated maximum, the car weighs 2 350 kg.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="5" data-ev>@@I make that assumption and use 2 350 kg throughout; every energy and gas figure below scales with it.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="6" data-ev>@@Tesla's 80 kN does not check it: that figure belongs to the rear thrusters, which push the car forward, and the 3.3 g peak on the gauge comes from the corner thrusters braking its fall.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="7">@@If the four corner thrusters were as strong as the four rear ones, 80 kN at 3.3 g would give 2,472 kg, consistent but not a measurement.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="8">@@Hagerty's 1.7 t is the car in the studio, which carries a 200-litre tank; the flight system adds another 400 litres of tank, six thrusters and their gas.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S2.p4" data-s="9">@@At the 0.6 kg per litre of composite 70 MPa hydrogen tanks, the extra tank weighs about 240 kg and its nitrogen about 200 kg, so the flying car would weigh about 2.1 t before its thrusters and plumbing, within about 10% of the figure I use.@@html:</span>@@

* The half loop

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The wall is close to a half circle.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Plotting the pitch gauge against the altitude gauge during the slow climb removes time from the problem and leaves geometry: a first arc of 9.1 m radius takes the car from the floor to vertical, a second of 9.8 m takes it to 170°, nearly upside down, and the altitude keeps rising to 21.1 m while the pitch reads 170°.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p1" data-s="2">@@Taken at face value, that last part is a straight inverted section about 13 m long; the frames suggest a shorter lip, so the altitude reference may sit above the road surface.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p1" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The arcs are the part I use.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Four forces act on the car on the wall: its weight @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>@@, the fans' suction @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>@@ pulling it toward the road, the road's normal force @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>@@ pushing it away, and the tyres' traction @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ along the road.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p2" data-s="1">@@With @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x003B8;</mi></mrow></math>@@ the angle of the road (0 on the floor, 90° vertical, 180° upside down) and @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>@@ its radius, Newton's second law across and along the road[fn:: Across the road the car follows a curve, and a body moving at speed v on a curve of radius R needs a net force m v²/R toward the centre of the curve. On the wall that centre lies on the car's roof side.] reads@@html:</span>@@

#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The tyres stay on the road while @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#x02265;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>@@, and they hold while @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#x0007C;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#x0007C;</mo><mo>&#x02264;</mo><mi>&#x003BC;</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>@@[fn:: The friction coefficient μ is the largest ratio of friction force to normal force a tyre carries before it slides: about 0.9 to 1.1 for road tyres on dry concrete, over 1.5 for racing slicks.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@For the slow climb, where @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>&#x02248;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>@@, the grip the tyres need is@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<div class="rf-math"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mrow><mi>&#x003BC;</mi><mo>&#x02265;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mi>&#x003B8;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>&#x0002F;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><mi>cos</mi><mi>&#x003B8;</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math></div>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@With suction equal to twice the weight, that requirement peaks at @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x003BC;</mi><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mn>0.58</mn></mrow></math>@@ at 120°, inside what a road tyre gives on dry concrete.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p4" data-s="1" data-ev>@@With suction equal to the weight it diverges as the car turns over: at 150° the car would need @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x003BC;</mi><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mn>3.7</mn></mrow></math>@@, and upside down no tyre holds.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p4" data-s="2" data-ev>@@"Two g" is the suction that lets a car crawl around a half loop with a margin of about 1.7 on grip.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p5" data-s="0">@@The fast run shows the same thing from the other side.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p5" data-s="1" data-ev>@@A car without suction going around a loop of radius 9.8 m needs at least @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>g</mi><mi>R</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>@@ = 9.8 m/s at the top, and therefore at least 21.5 m/s at the bottom.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p5" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Inverting the altitude record through the wall profile gives the Roadster's speed on the two arcs: between 5 and 10 m/s, 6.1 m/s on average, covering their 28 m in 4.0 s.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p5" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The suction carries what speed would otherwise have to.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p6" data-s="0" data-ev>@@As a check on the gauge itself, the specific force those speeds imply, @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#x0002F;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><mi>g</mi><mi>cos</mi><mi>&#x003B8;</mi></mrow></math>@@ across the road and the drive force along it, matches the G-force gauge to 0.4 g RMS.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S3.p6" data-s="1" data-ev>@@That is too loose to recover the speed from the gauge, but it says the gauge is reading the car and not decoration.@@html:</span>@@

* Energy

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S4.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Mass appears in every energy and in no speed.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S4.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The car's speeds are the measured quantities; the energies below scale with the 2 350 kg I assumed.@@html:</span>@@

| Quantity | Value |
|---+---|
| Potential energy at the top of the wall | 485 kJ (0.13 kWh) |
| Free-fall speed after 21.1 m | 20.3 m/s |
| Fastest measured descent | 15.0 m/s |
| Kinetic energy at that speed | 263 kJ, removed by the thrusters in about a second |
| Potential energy at the kickflip apex | 184 kJ |
| Launch speed needed for that apex, with the 0.2 g of lift the gauge shows during the coast | 11.1 m/s |

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S4.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Climbing the wall costs the battery at least 0.13 kWh.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S4.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The flight is the expensive part, and its energy comes from the tank.@@html:</span>@@

* Nitrogen at 10 000 psi

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p1" data-s="0">@@Ten thousand psi is 68.9 MPa, 680 atmospheres.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@At that pressure nitrogen is far from an ideal gas.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p1" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The ideal-gas law puts 475 kg of nitrogen in 600 litres at 20 °C; the reference equation of state for nitrogen [cite:@span2000nitrogen], evaluated with CoolProp [cite:@bell2014coolprop], gives 495 kg/m³ and 297 kg.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p1" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The compressibility factor is 1.60[fn:: The compressibility factor Z = p/(ρRT) compares a real gas with an ideal one. At Z = 1 the gas is ideal; above 1 the molecules' repulsion makes it stiffer than the ideal-gas law predicts, so less of it fits in the tank.]: the molecules sit close enough that their repulsion holds the volume open.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p1" data-s="4">@@Air, on the equation of state for air [cite:@lemmon2000air], gives 319 kg.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@That nitrogen is a supercritical fluid[fn:: Above its critical temperature and pressure a substance has no boiling point: compressed further, it grows denser continuously and never forms a liquid surface. Supercritical carbon dioxide, above 31 °C and 7.4 MPa, is one of the solvents used to take the caffeine out of coffee.], which is a different thing from a superfluid.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p2" data-s="1">@@Nitrogen's critical point is 126.2 K and 3.40 MPa; the tank sits at 2.3 times the critical temperature and 20 times the critical pressure.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@There the distinction between liquid and gas disappears: the fluid in the tank is 495 kg/m³, 61% as dense as liquid nitrogen at its boiling point, but it fills the tank like a gas, with no surface, no bubbles and no boiling.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p2" data-s="3">@@A superfluid is a quantum liquid that flows with zero viscosity[fn:: Superfluid helium-4 creeps up the walls of its container, leaks through pores a few nanometres wide, and keeps flowing around a ring without slowing down. A large share of its atoms share one quantum state, which takes very light atoms at very low temperature.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p2" data-s="4" data-ev>@@Helium-4 becomes one below 2.17 K [cite:@kapitza1938viscosity; @allen1938flow]; nitrogen freezes at 63 K long before quantum effects could matter, so nitrogen is never superfluid.@@html:</span>@@

y="97.5" text-anchor="start">supercritical fluid</text></g></svg><figcaption>Nitrogen's phase diagram over its whole range, computed with CoolProp from the reference equation of state of Span and colleagues (2000) and its melting and sublimation equations. Below the triple point, 63.2 K and 12.5 kPa, the solid sublimes; between the triple point and the critical point the liquid boils; above the critical point the fluid is supercritical until a pressure of about 2.3 GPa at room temperature freezes it. The melting curve is dashed where it is extrapolated past 287 K, and the dashed line at 35.6 K separates the two solid forms, α and β. The tank sits in the supercritical region, far from the solid.</figcaption></figure>

The full tank sits deep in the supercritical region. If the tank empties without taking heat from its walls, the gas left behind cools along the orange path toward the critical point. The gas fed to a thruster expands in the nozzle along the blue path and ends inside the liquid-vapour region at 77 K.</figcaption></figure>

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Three things happen to that gas on its way out.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The regulator drops it to the thruster's chamber pressure; I assume 20 MPa.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p4" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Throttling keeps the enthalpy[fn:: Enthalpy, h = u + p/ρ, is a fluid's internal energy plus the work it does pushing its way into a space. When gas passes through a valve without exchanging heat or work, its enthalpy is the same on both sides.] constant, and at these pressures throttling warms nitrogen slightly instead of cooling it[fn:: This is the Joule-Thomson effect. Most gases cool when throttled, because their molecules attract and pulling them apart costs energy; refrigerators and gas liquefiers work this way. At high enough pressure the molecules' repulsion dominates and the gas warms instead. The boundary is called the inversion curve, and this tank starts above it.], so with a full tank it leaves the regulator at 294 K, about one kelvin warmer than it went in.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p4" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Once the tank falls below about 40 MPa the same valve cools the gas instead.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p5" data-s="0">@@The nozzle accelerates it.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p5" data-s="1" data-ev>@@An ideal expansion from 20 MPa to one atmosphere gives an exhaust speed of 656 m/s, a specific impulse of 67 s[fn:: Thrust is the momentum the nozzle throws backwards each second, F = ṁ v_e, plus a pressure term that is zero for an ideal nozzle. Specific impulse is the exhaust speed divided by standard gravity, 9.81 m/s²: the seconds one kilogram of propellant can hold up its own weight. Cold nitrogen gives about 70 s; a kerosene and oxygen rocket engine about 300 s.], and a thrust coefficient of 1.60[fn:: The thrust coefficient C_F = F/(p_c A_t) measures how well a nozzle turns chamber pressure p_c, acting on the throat area A_t, into thrust. An ideal nozzle expanding nitrogen from 20 MPa to one atmosphere gives 1.6.] [cite:@sutton2016rocket].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p5" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The exhaust leaves at 77 K with about 89% of it still vapour; the rest condenses into droplets.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p5" data-s="3">@@The white plumes in the video are probably that mist mixed with condensed moisture from the air, though the stage also used fog, and I cannot tell the three apart.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p6" data-s="0">@@The tank cools.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p6" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Each kilogram that leaves does work pushing the rest out, and if the walls supply no heat the gas left behind follows an isentrope[fn:: Adiabatic means no heat crosses the boundary; isentropic means adiabatic and without friction or mixing, so the entropy stays constant. A gas that expands isentropically does work on whatever it pushes and cools down.]: after a third of the gas is used the tank drops below a 20 MPa regulator setting, and after 40% it is at 200 K and 15 MPa.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p6" data-s="2">@@Composite tanks have polymer liners that insulate, so the real tank sits somewhere between this adiabatic path and room temperature.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p6" data-s="3" data-ev>@@Below the regulator setting the thrust falls with the tank's pressure, so a tank that cools loses thrust within a single stunt.@@html:</span>@@

The regulator moves the gas along a line of constant enthalpy (green). If no heat reaches it, the gas left in the tank cools straight down at constant entropy (orange) toward the critical point. The nozzle expands its gas at constant entropy (blue) from 20 MPa to one atmosphere and ends inside the dome, where liquid and vapour coexist.</figcaption></figure>

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p7" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The peak of 76 kN shared by four corner thrusters is 19 kN each.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p7" data-s="1" data-ev>@@At 20 MPa that needs a throat of 5.9 cm², 2.8 cm across, and all four together swallow 116 kg of nitrogen a second.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p7" data-s="2" data-ev>@@At that rate the full tank lasts 2.6 s.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="0">@@The gauge also tells us how much nitrogen each stunt used.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="1">@@The G-force gauge reads thrust per unit of the car's weight, so the integral of its reading over a flight, times the car's weight, is the thrust impulse, and dividing by the exhaust speed gives the gas.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="2">@@I integrate only while the car is in the air; on its wheels the accelerometer reads the road's support, not thrust.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The kickflip's lift burns used 120 kg and the descent off the wall 163 kg, 55% of the tank.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="4" data-ev>@@The accelerometer cannot see a pure torque, so the roll adds roughly 41 kg, which brings the kickflip to about the same as the descent.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="5">@@With 10% uncertainty in the mass and 5% in the exhaust speed, the mass of gas alone might stretch to two stunts.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="6">@@Pressure settles it.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="7" data-ev>@@The thrusters need the regulator's 20 MPa, and the tank stays above that only until a third of its gas is gone if it cools as it empties, or a little over half if its walls keep it warm.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="8">@@One stunt uses about half.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p8" data-s="9" data-ev>@@A full 600-litre tank is one stunt, not several, and the car must refill between them.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p9" data-s="0">@@Refilling is not free.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p9" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The least work that can compress nitrogen from the atmosphere into that tank is its exergy[fn:: Exergy is the most work a substance can deliver as it comes into equilibrium with its surroundings, and so also the least work it takes to put it in that state. For a gas compressed at room temperature it is the rise in enthalpy plus the room temperature times the fall in entropy.], 595 kJ per kilogram, or 49 kWh for the whole tank.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p9" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Real compressors reach perhaps half to two thirds of that ideal, so a refill costs something like 70 to 100 kWh, comparable to the whole battery of most electric cars, for one stunt.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p9" data-s="3" data-ev>@@Hagerty's presenter adds that filling all 600 litres takes six to seven hours today, that it is not something done at home, and that Tesla is working to bring it down to about half an hour [cite:@hagerty2026roadster].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p9" data-s="4" data-ev>@@Over six and a half hours that refill draws 11 to 15 kW on average; in half an hour it would draw 140 to 200 kW.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S5.p9" data-s="5" data-ev>@@Musk said on stage that the car recharges its tank itself, but a refill that cannot be done at home suggests that, for now, the compressor is not in the car.@@html:</span>@@

* The kickflip

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The kickflip is a roll about the car's long axis.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p1" data-s="1">@@Seen from behind, the car's corner thrusters push along the car's own up axis: they can push and never pull.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p1" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Their difference makes a torque, @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#x02212;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo><mspace width="0.167em" /><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>@@, with @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#x02248;</mo></mrow></math>@@ 0.85 m, half the distance between the left and right corners.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p1" data-s="3" data-ev>@@Their sum makes a force along the car's up axis, and once the car is upside down that force points at the ground.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="0">@@So the corners can roll the car, but every newton-metre they make comes with a push, and for half the roll that push is aimed at the ground.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The gauges say the car does not pay that price.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@If the corners made all the torque the measured roll needs (below), the G-force gauge would read at least 1.1 g at the roll's peak; through the roll it reads about 0.2 g.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="3" data-ev>@@For the corners alone to fit that reading, the car's roll inertia would have to be below 279 kg·m², a radius of gyration of 34 cm, far easier to roll than a car of this size can be.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="4" data-ev>@@So the car makes torque in some way that adds little net force, and Moravy's list of nozzles does not say how.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="5">@@Musk spoke of "attitude control thrusters", and mid-roll the frames show plumes leaving the corners sideways, which canted corner nozzles would produce.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p2" data-s="6" data-ev>@@I model the source as a couple[fn:: A couple is two equal and opposite forces that do not act along the same line. They add to zero, so they do not move the centre of mass, but they turn the body; the torque is either force times the distance between their lines.], @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@, a torque with no net force, and the simulators below let you switch it off and fly on the corners alone.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The roll itself I read from the HUD's attitude icon.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p3" data-s="1">@@A turn that starts and ends at rest must speed up and then brake, so I fitted a profile with those end conditions built in: a minimum-jerk curve[fn:: Jerk is the rate of change of acceleration. A minimum-jerk curve is the smoothest way to move from rest to rest in a given time; human arm movements follow it closely.] plus two shape terms that vanish, with their first two derivatives, at both ends.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The fit has the roll start 285.5 s into CNET's cut and take 2.1 s: the car turns its first half-turn in about 0.8 s, almost stops while upside down, and turns the second half in another 0.8 s.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p3" data-s="3">@@The turn rate peaks at 6.0 rad/s.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p3" data-s="4" data-ev>@@Treating the car as a uniform box of 2.0 by 1.2 m gives a roll inertia[fn:: The moment of inertia is to rotation what mass is to a push: torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. For a uniform box of mass m, width w and height h rolling about its long axis, it is m(w² + h²)/12.] of 1,065 kg·m², an upper estimate for a car that carries its battery in the floor, and the torque the profile needs peaks at 22 kN·m, which from the corners alone would take a difference of 26 kN, more than one corner thruster's 19 kN.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The same reading settles how the car turns upright after it leaves the wall.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p4" data-s="1">@@It goes from 170° to level in 1.5 s.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p4" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Done as a roll, that needs 12 kN·m; done end over end, as a pitch, the inertia is 4,073 kg·m² and the torque 46 kN·m, nearly four times as much.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S6.p4" data-s="3" data-ev>@@A car is much easier to roll than to flip end over end, so I take the turn off the wall to be a roll and model both stunts in the roll plane.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@subject to @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#x02264;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>&#x0002C;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>&#x02264;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>@@ and @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#x0007C;</mo><msub><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#x0007C;</mo><mo>&#x02264;</mo><msub><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>@@, where @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ collects what the controller does not command: a misaligned nozzle, a gust, the fans' wake.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The valves do not deliver a command at once; each thrust follows its command through a lag of about 30 ms, @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mover><mi>F</mi><mo>&#x002D9;</mo></mover><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x02212;</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>@@.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The controller measures @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x003C6;</mi></mrow></math>@@ with noise, 100 times a second.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The rotational part does not depend on the translation.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p4" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Its transfer function[fn:: A transfer function describes a linear system as the ratio of output to input after a Laplace transform, in which s stands for differentiation and 1/s for integration. So 1/(I s²) reads as divide by I and integrate twice; e^(−sT) is a pure delay of T seconds; 1/(T s + 1) is a lag that covers 63% of a step in T seconds.] from commanded torque to roll angle is a double integrator behind the valve lag and any delay @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@:@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<div class="rf-math"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#x003C6;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#x02212;</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.167em" /><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mi>s</mi><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math></div>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p5" data-s="0" data-ev>@@A double integrator never settles on its own and has no damping: any constant torque error grows into an angle error quadratically.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S7.p5" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The coupling runs the other way: the translation depends on @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x003C6;</mi></mrow></math>@@ through @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mi>&#x003C6;</mi></mrow></math>@@ and @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mi>&#x003C6;</mi></mrow></math>@@, so a roll error turns into a sideways drift and a loss of lift.@@html:</span>@@

* The controller

The reference is the measured roll; the PID with feed-forward computes a torque; the allocation sends it to the couple first and to the corner pair only when the car is upright enough for their net force to help.</figcaption></figure>

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The attitude controller, the loop that turns the car to the roll angle the plan asks for, is a PID on the roll error[fn:: Feedback means acting on the measured error. It corrects whatever happens, including what nobody modelled, but only after the error has appeared.] with a feed-forward term[fn:: Feed-forward means acting on the plan instead of the error: the controller applies the torque the reference needs before any error appears. It is fast but blind to surprises, so controllers pair it with feedback, which is slower but sees them.], normalised by the inertia so that the gains are in units of frequency:@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<div class="rf-math"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C4;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">&#x00028;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em" /><mi>e</mi><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x0222B;</mo><mi>e</mi><mspace width="0.167em" /><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em" /><mover><mi>e</mi><mo>&#x002D9;</mo></mover><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><msub><mover><mi>&#x003C6;</mi><mo>&#x000A8;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">&#x00029;</mo></mrow><mo>&#x0002C;</mo><mspace width="2em" /><mi>e</mi><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><msub><mi>&#x003C6;</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x02212;</mo><msub><mi>&#x003C6;</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math></div>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The feed-forward term is the torque the reference needs if everything goes to plan, computed from the reference itself.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The PID terms correct what the plan got wrong[fn:: The proportional term pushes against the present error; the integral against the error accumulated so far, which removes steady offsets; the derivative against the error's rate of change, which damps the motion.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@I clamp the integral so that it cannot wind up[fn:: When the thrusters are at their limit the error persists and the integral keeps growing. When the error finally reverses, the oversized integral throws the car past its target. Clamping the integral prevents this windup.] while the actuators saturate, and take the derivative as a finite difference of the sampled error.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p3" data-s="0">@@The allocation turns a torque and a collective force into thruster commands.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Torque goes to the couple up to its limit.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Whatever is left goes to the corner pair as a difference, but only while the car is within 72° of upright; past that, the corner pair's net force would push the car sideways or down.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p3" data-s="3" data-ev>@@If a split would need a negative thrust on one side, that side shuts and the other makes the torque alone.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p4" data-s="0">@@The collective force has its own small logic, one rule per phase.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p4" data-s="1" data-ev>@@For the kickflip: a launch burn, then the measured 0.2 g of residual lift while the car coasts, then a landing law.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p4" data-s="2">@@Within 30° of upright the corner pair makes it.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p4" data-s="3" data-ev>@@Past that none of the nozzles Tesla lists can push up and I cannot see what does, so the model applies it there as a vertical force.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p4" data-s="4" data-ev>@@For the descent off the wall: no thrust while the car turns upright, then a lander's sink-rate law, which commands a vertical speed that falls with height,@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<div class="rf-math"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mo>&#x02212;</mo><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.167em" /><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.167em" /><mo stretchy="false">&#x00028;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x02212;</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#x00029;</mo></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math></div>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p5" data-s="0" data-ev>@@a constant deceleration @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ down to a gate at @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ = 3 m and @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ = −2 m/s, then a linear slow-down to 1 m/s at contact.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p5" data-s="1" data-ev>@@A PI loop on the error in vertical speed sets the thrust, divided by @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mi>&#x003C6;</mi></mrow></math>@@ so that a tilted car still holds its vertical rate.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p5" data-s="2" data-ev>@@A proportional tilt on the horizontal speed brings the sideways drift to zero.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p6" data-s="0" data-ev>@@In the simulator the PID is five lines, run every 10 ms:@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<pre class="rf-code"><code>err = ref - a_meas
derr = 0.0 if prev_err is None else (err - prev_err) / p.ctrl_dt
prev_err = err
integ = max(-p.i_limit, min(p.i_limit, integ + err * p.ctrl_dt))
tau = inertia * (
    p.kp * err
    + p.ki * integ
    + p.kd * derr
    + (ref_acc if p.feedforward else 0.0)
)</code></pre>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S8.p7" data-s="0" data-ev>@@and the allocation is a function that knows the thrusters can only push:@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<pre class="rf-code"><code>def allocate(
    collective: float, tau: float, arm: float, cap: float
) -&gt; tuple[float, float]:
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Split a collective force and a torque between two push-only groups.

    Torque wins: if the split would need a negative thrust, that group is shut
    and the other alone makes the torque, adding |tau|/arm of net force.
    &quot;&quot;&quot;
    half = tau / (2 * arm)
    fa, fb = collective / 2 - half, collective / 2 + half
    if fa &lt; 0:
        fa, fb = 0.0, abs(tau) / arm if tau &gt; 0 else 0.0
    if fb &lt; 0:
        fa, fb = abs(tau) / arm if tau &lt; 0 else 0.0, 0.0
    return min(max(fa, 0.0), cap), min(max(fb, 0.0), cap)</code></pre>
#+end_export

* Tuning

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@With the gains normalised by the inertia, the closed rotational loop, ignoring the valve lag, has the characteristic polynomial @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mi>s</mi><mo>&#x0002B;</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p1" data-s="1">@@Choosing@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<div class="rf-math"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#x0002C;</mo><mspace width="2em" /><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mspace width="0.167em" /><msub><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x0002C;</mo><mspace width="2em" /><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#x0002F;</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math></div>
#+end_export

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@places two poles close to the natural frequency, at @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.93</mn><mspace width="0.167em" /><msub><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ with damping 0.75[fn:: In a second-order loop the natural frequency sets how quickly it responds and the damping ratio how much it overshoots. A damping ratio of 0.7 to 0.8 gives 2 to 5% overshoot and no ringing. That holds for a pure second-order loop. This one also has the PID's zeros, which make a bare step in the reference overshoot by about 20%; a planned turn with feed-forward never asks for a step.] and a third, slow pole near @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x0002F;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>@@ that removes steady errors [cite:@astrom2021feedback].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@That leaves one number to choose.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@Ziegler and Nichols' rules [cite:@ziegler1942optimum] tune from a measured step response or from the gain at which the loop oscillates; a double integrator has neither, so pole placement is the natural method here.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Faster is better until delay catches up.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The valve lag and the sampling period already cost phase, and each millisecond of extra latency costs more at higher frequency[fn:: A delay of T seconds shifts a sinusoid of angular frequency ω by ωT radians. Once a correction arrives half a cycle late it adds to the error instead of cancelling it, and the loop oscillates. Every loop has some delay, so every loop has a highest frequency it can work at.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@I swept @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ for three latencies:@@html:</span>@@

#+begin_export html
<figure class="rf" id="fig-sweep"><svg class="rf-fig" viewBox="0 0 660 362" role="img" aria-labelledby="t d" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><title>Bandwidth against delay</title><desc>Worst roll error during the simulated kickflip against the PID loop&#x27;s natural frequency, for three amounts of extra latency. Crosses mark runs where the car did not land.</desc><g class="panel" data-panel="{&quot;x0&quot;: 64, &quot;x1&quot;: 634, &quot;y0&quot;: 58, &quot;y1&quot;: 318, &quot;xlim&quot;: [2, 28], &quot;ylim&quot;: [0, 120], &quot;series&quot;: [{&quot;name&quot;: &quot;no extra delay&quot;, &quot;cls&quot;: &quot;s1&quot;, &quot;unit&quot;: &quot;deg&quot;, &quot;x&quot;: [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28], &quot;y&quot;: [31.0, 15.1, 10.3, 7.9, 6.1, 3.9, 3.8, 3.9, 3.6, 3.4, 3.6, 3.4, 5.2, 17.8]}, {&quot;name&quot;: &quot;30 ms extra&quot;, &quot;cls&quot;: &quot;s2&quot;, &quot;unit&quot;: &quot;deg&quot;, &quot;x&quot;: [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28], &quot;y&quot;: [36.6, 23.1, 18.3, 14.3, 11.5, 9.3, 7.6, 10.2, 46.0, 215.0, 229.4, 226.2, 467.9, 604.4]}, {&quot;name&quot;: &quot;60 ms extra&quot;, &quot;cls&quot;: &quot;s3&quot;, &quot;unit&quot;: &quot;deg&quot;, &quot;x&quot;: [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Without extra latency the error falls until about 16 rad/s.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="1">@@Past that the derivative term turns sensor noise into torque demands larger than the couple's 30 kN·m, and the excess goes to the corner pair.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="2" data-ev>@@During the launch both corners are at full thrust, so the only way they can make a difference is to throttle one side down: from 20 rad/s the car loses enough lift that it no longer reaches the 6 m it needs to clear the row, though it still lands upright and slow.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="3" data-ev>@@With 30 ms extra it fails beyond 12 rad/s, and with 60 ms beyond 8.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="4">@@Noise sets the other limit: the derivative term multiplies the measurement noise by @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#x0002F;</mo><mi>&#x00394;</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>@@, and that torque is real gas spent on nothing.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="5" data-ev>@@I chose @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x003C9;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ = 8 rad/s, which gives @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ = 64 s⁻², @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ = 12 s⁻¹ and @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>@@ = 512/12 ≈ 43 s⁻³, which I round to 40.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S9.p4" data-s="6">@@It sits well inside the delay limit and leaves room for noise.@@html:</span>@@

* The model against the measurement

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The controller structure is mine; the size of each burn is the car's, and the telemetry pins it.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@I fitted the kickflip's launch burn and the descent's braking level by least squares on the gauge altitude[fn:: This is system identification: choosing a model's unknown parameters so that its output matches measured data. Here the parameters are the size and length of the launch burn and the braking level of the descent, and the data are the altitude gauge.].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p1" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The launch comes out as 3.3 g for 0.44 s, close to the 3.2 g the gauge shows at lift-off, and the braking as a design deceleration of 1.1 g.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p1" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The descent fits best with no lift burn while the car turns upright.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p1" data-s="4">@@The gauge shows 0.3 to 0.5 g in that half second and the right corner lamps are lit, so the car is firing; the fit says that push is too small, or points too far sideways, to change its height much.@@html:</span>@@

Altitude matches to 0.30 m RMS on the kickflip and 0.55 m on the descent; the controller tracks the turn fitted to the HUD icon to within 4° on the kickflip and 5° on the descent. Once the descent's turn is done the controller tilts the car up to 9° against its sideways speed, which the fitted turn does not include.</figcaption></figure>
#+end_export

| | Kickflip | Descent off the wall |
|---+---+---|
| Altitude error against the gauge, RMS | 0.30 m | 0.55 m |
| Worst roll tracking error | 4.0° | 5.3° |
| Touchdown | 1.6 m/s, 0.0° off level | 1.4 m/s, 0.1° off level |
| Nitrogen, simulated | 174 kg | 154 kg |
| Nitrogen, from the gauge | 120 kg, plus about 41 kg for the roll | 163 kg |
| Peak specific force, simulated and measured | 3.3 g and 3.2 g | 2.5 g and 3.3 g |

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The simulated nitrogen agrees with the gauge estimate to within 8%, inside the uncertainty of the mass and the exhaust speed.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p2" data-s="1">@@Two disagreements are worth stating, and the figures below show both.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The real car brakes sooner and harder than my sink-rate law: off the wall the gauge passes 1.5 g at 12.1 m and peaks at 3.3 g at 6.7 m, where the PID passes 1.5 g at 9.6 m and peaks at 2.5 g at its 3 m gate.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p2" data-s="3" data-ev>@@Tesla's controller takes most of the speed off high up and then sinks slowly through the last few metres.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S10.p2" data-s="4" data-ev>@@And the real car lights its corner thrusters while it turns, where my allocation sends the torque to the couple first.@@html:</span>@@

simulation</text></svg><figcaption>What the PID decides against what the car did, kickflip. Gold: a thruster lamp lit on the HUD. Blue: the thrust each group of the simulated PID makes, as a share of the most it can make. Both launch on all four corners. During the roll the PID uses the couple alone, as its allocation is written to; the car lights its left and right corners in alternating bursts. The car also starts its landing burn higher, passing 1.5 g at 4.6 m against the PID's 3.2 m, and brakes harder, 2.5 g against 1.7 g. The nose lamps are the two yaw thrusters, which this planar model leaves out; the bottom row shows the couple the model uses instead.</figcaption></figure>

class="legend" x="174.0" y="528.0">measured, HUD</text><line class="s1" x1="271.0" x2="289.0" y1="524.0" y2="524.0" stroke-width="2.5"/><text class="legend" x="295.0" y="528.0">PID simulation</text></svg><figcaption>The same comparison for the descent off the half loop. The car lights its right corners as it leaves the top and both sides from 0.4 s, while it turns upright; the PID turns with the couple alone and fires its corner pair from about 1.2 s, once it is upright. The car then brakes sooner and harder, peaking at 3.3 g at 6.7 m against the PID's 2.5 g at 3.0 m.</figcaption></figure>

* Sideways drift

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@In the kickflip the car also moves sideways, and it is fair to ask whether anyone controlled that.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p1" data-s="1">@@Two cameras help, and they see different things.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p1" data-s="2">@@Tesla's far shot sees the car side-on and the parked row end-on: there the large horizontal motion is the car travelling forward along its own axis, which is the jump that clears the row.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p1" data-s="3" data-ev>@@The livestream's wide shot sees the car end-on during the first half of the roll, so the horizontal motion there is sideways: about half a metre in the first 0.75 s, measured against the Semi with the car's own width as the ruler.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p1" data-s="4">@@In the second half the car turns side-on to that camera, so it also yaws by about 90° while it rolls, which my planar model cannot represent.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p1" data-s="5" data-ev>@@My best estimate of the total sideways drift is one to two metres; the cameras do not allow a better one.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The simulation drifts too, 1.7 m by touchdown, and the cause is the coupling in the equations of motion.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p2" data-s="1">@@The only sideways force the car can make is its lift tilted with the body, @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mover><mi>h</mi><mo>&#x000A8;</mo></mover><mo>&#x0003D;</mo><mo>&#x02212;</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>&#x003C6;</mi></mrow></math>@@.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@During the 3.3 g launch, the nozzle bias and the sensor noise hold the car about 1° off level, and 1° of a 76 kN burn pushes 2 350 kg sideways at 0.56 m/s².@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p2" data-s="3">@@The residual lift adds a few tenths of a metre per second as the roll starts.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p2" data-s="4" data-ev>@@Once the car is rolling nothing can push it back: the lift is off and the couple makes torque, not force.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p2" data-s="5">@@The car crosses the row carrying about half a metre per second sideways for three seconds.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Holding the sideways position means tilting against the drift, and the car can only do that once it is upright again, with about 1.3 s left and a tilt it would rather not have at touchdown.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@With a sideways-hold loop the simulated kickflip lands 1.2 m from its line instead of 1.7 m, and 1° off level instead of level.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The descent off the wall has more time after the turn, and the same loop brings its offset from 2.8 m to 0.9 m, starting from the rough 1.5 m/s of sideways speed I assumed.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p4" data-s="0" data-ev>@@So the drift is easy to explain and hard to remove with a loop per axis.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p4" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The car is underactuated[fn:: A system is underactuated when it has fewer independent controls than coordinates to control. A car on a road is one: it cannot move sideways directly, which is why parallel parking takes several manoeuvres.]: three coordinates and, during the roll, only one way to make a force.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p4" data-s="2" data-ev>@@This is the planar vertical take-off and landing aircraft of the control literature [cite:@hauser1992pvtol], and the known remedy is to plan the position and the attitude together instead of controlling them one by one.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p4" data-s="3">@@A trajectory can be chosen so that the sideways impulses of the launch and the landing cancel [cite:@fliess1995flatness; @martin1996vtol].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p4" data-s="4">@@Planning position and attitude together is also how quadcopters fly aggressive paths through narrow gaps [cite:@mellinger2011minimum], and adjusting a planned manoeuvre from one flight to the next lets them chain several flips [cite:@lupashin2010flips].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S11.p4" data-s="5" data-ev>@@My guess is that Tesla left the drift alone: on an empty lot, landing a metre to one side costs nothing, and landing tilted costs a lot.@@html:</span>@@

* Fly it

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S12.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Both simulators below run the same model as the analysis, ported line by line to JavaScript and checked against it to six significant figures.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S12.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Change a gain or a toggle and the page recomputes the flight; press fly to watch it.@@html:</span>@@

simulator needs JavaScript.</p></noscript></div><figcaption>The kickflip. The car and the blue curves are the simulated flight with the settings above; the orange curves are the livestream gauges. Every change re-runs the flight; press fly to watch it, or drag the time bar. Things to try: untick feed-forward and the worst roll error grows from 4° to 21°, because the PID learns about the turn only after the car has fallen behind it. Set K_p to 0 and the feed-forward still flies the roll, 17° off at worst. Raise the sensor noise to 3° and the derivative term turns noise into thrust: the car lands 45° over at 7.1 m/s. Untick the couple τ<sub>c</sub> and the corner thrusters make all the torque, as Tesla's list of nozzles has it; upside down they push the car toward the ground, which it hits at 9.1 m/s. Tick hold sideways position and the car lands 1.2 m from its line instead of 1.7 m, 1° tilted.<dl><dt>K_p, K_i, K_d</dt><dd>The PID gains, divided by the inertia so that they are frequencies. K_p pushes against the present roll error, K_i against the error accumulated so far, K_d against its rate of change.</dd><dt>extra latency</dt><dd>Delay between the controller and the valves, on top of the 30 ms valve lag and the 10 ms control period.</dd><dt>sensor noise</dt><dd>Standard deviation of the roll angle the controller measures, 100 times a second.</dd><dt>misaligned nozzle</dt><dd>A constant torque the controller does not know about.</dd><dt>gust for 0.3 s</dt><dd>A torque pulse, 1.2 s into the kickflip and 0.6 s into the descent.</dd><dt>launch burn, design braking</dt><dd>The lift-off thrust of the kickflip; the deceleration the descent's sink-rate law plans for above 3 m.</dd><dt>feed-forward</dt><dd>Adds the torque the planned turn needs before any error appears.</dd><dt>couple τ<sub>c</sub></dt><dd>Torque without lift, up to 30 kN·m, that the gauges require and Tesla's list of nozzles does not name. Unticked, the corner pair makes all the torque, at any angle.</dd><dt>on/off valves</dt><dd>Each valve fully open or shut, pulsed 100 times a second so that the pulses average to the command.</dd><dt>tank cools as it empties</dt><dd>The gas left in the tank expands with no heat from the walls, so pressure and thrust fall as the stunt goes on.</dd><dt>second stunt</dt><dd>The tank starts at 45%, about what one stunt leaves, and already cold.</dd><dt>measured reference</dt><dd>The planned turn is the one read off the HUD icon; unticked, a smooth minimum-jerk turn.</dd><dt>hold sideways position</dt><dd>Once upright again, tilt against the sideways offset as well as the sideways speed.</dd></dl></figcaption></figure>

simulator needs JavaScript.</p></noscript></div><figcaption>The descent off the half loop, from the moment the car leaves the top upside down; the controls are the same as above. Things to try: tick second stunt and the tank starts at 45% and cold, the thrust the sink-rate law expects is not there, and the car hits the ground at 16 m/s. Set design braking to 0.7 g and the car hovers longer and spends 166 kg of nitrogen; at 2.0 g it spends 144 kg and lands at 1.5 m/s. A 30 kN·m gust throws the turn 33° off its plan, and the car still lands. Untick the couple τ<sub>c</sub> and it lands too, 8.3 m to the side.</figcaption></figure>

* Failure cases for the PID

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The PID flies both stunts in simulation.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@Here is what happens when the assumptions behind it fail, one at a time:@@html:</span>@@

| Change | Kickflip | Descent |
|---+---+---|
| None (the settings above) | lands, 1.6 m/s | lands, 1.4 m/s |
| On/off valves, modulated at 100 Hz | lands, 1.6 m/s | lands, 1.3 m/s |
| No feed-forward | lands, worst error 21° | lands, worst error 14° |
| 6 kN·m nozzle bias, no integral | lands 5.1° tilted | lands 0.1° tilted |
| 6 kN·m nozzle bias, with integral | lands 0.1° tilted | lands 0.1° tilted |
| 50 ms extra latency | lands, worst error 20° | lands, 200 kg of nitrogen |
| 120 ms extra latency | roll diverges, lands 158° over | lands on its side |
| Sensor noise 3° | lands 45° over | lands, 268 kg of nitrogen |
| Corner thrusters only, as Tesla lists them | hits at 9.1 m/s | lands, 1.3 m/s, 8.3 m to the side |
| Tank cools as it empties | hits at 5.9 m/s | hits at 3.1 m/s |
| Second stunt: the tank one stunt leaves, cold | never leaves the ground | hits at 16 m/s |
| Sideways hold after the turn | lands 1.2 m to the side, not 1.7 m | lands 0.9 m to the side, not 2.8 m |

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The PID handles four of these.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="1">@@On/off valves change nothing, because 100 Hz modulation and a 30 ms lag average the pulses into the thrust the controller asked for.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="2">@@A constant bias is what the integral term is for.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="3">@@It tolerates 50 ms of extra latency, and it survives losing the feed-forward at a cost in accuracy.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="4" data-ev>@@Large latency, heavy sensor noise, the corner thrusters alone and a cooling tank break it.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="5">@@Latency and noise break any feedback loop past some bandwidth.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="6" data-ev>@@The last two share a cause: a PID reacts to the error it sees now.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="7">@@It does not know that the tank has less to give than it had a second ago, that the ground is three metres away, or that the torque it is about to ask for comes with a push toward that ground.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p2" data-s="8" data-ev>@@It cannot plan.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The model also leaves out things a real car has to deal with.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p3" data-s="1" data-ev>@@It is planar; the real car rolls, pitches and yaws together, and a controller written on Euler angles fails when the pitch reaches 90°[fn:: Euler angles describe attitude as three successive rotations. At 90° of pitch two of the three axes line up and one degree of freedom disappears; this is gimbal lock, and the equations divide by the cosine of the pitch. Quaternions, four numbers on a unit sphere, describe every attitude without such a point.], which this car passes through on the wall.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p3" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The car's four spinning wheels are gyroscopes: at 20 rad/s, four wheels of roughly 1 kg·m² carry 80 N·m·s of angular momentum, and rolling at 6 rad/s turns that into about 500 N·m of yaw torque, small next to 22 kN·m but a coupling a per-axis loop ignores.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p3" data-s="3">@@The fans' downforce has to hand over to the thrusters as the car leaves the wall.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p3" data-s="4">@@Plumes reflected off the ground change the thrust in the last metre.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S13.p3" data-s="5" data-ev>@@And the controller needs to know where the car is: an inertial unit drifts, so something has to measure height and attitude independently[fn:: The standard tool is a Kalman filter, which blends a model's prediction with noisy measurements, weighting each by its uncertainty, to estimate quantities that no single sensor measures well.].@@html:</span>@@

* A likely flight-control stack

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p1" data-s="0" data-ev>@@Tesla has not said, so this section is inference.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p1" data-s="1" data-ev>@@The presenters credited SpaceX with "the rest", and Lars Blackmore of SpaceX has described how the company lands rockets: a convex optimisation solved on board in a fraction of a second, with a solver generated by CVXGEN [cite:@blackmore2016autonomous].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p1" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The problem behind it is powered-descent guidance: the thrust history that uses the least propellant while respecting the thrust limits, a pointing limit, the ground and a soft touchdown.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p1" data-s="3">@@It is non-convex because a rocket engine cannot throttle below some minimum, and the method that made it solvable in milliseconds proves that a convex[fn:: A problem is convex when the set of allowed solutions has no dents and the cost has a single valley. Any local optimum is then the global one, and a solver finds it reliably in a bounded time, which is what a flight computer needs.] relaxation of the thrust constraint is exact at the optimum [cite:@acikmese2007convex].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p1" data-s="4">@@Code generators such as CVXGEN turn such a problem into a solver small and fast enough for a flight computer [cite:@mattingley2012cvxgen], and successive convexification extends it to the full six-degree-of-freedom problem [cite:@szmuk2018successive].@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p1" data-s="5" data-ev>@@Re-solving the problem from the measured state at every step is model predictive control[fn:: Model predictive control plans the next few seconds with a model, applies only the first step of the plan, measures where the car really is, and plans again. The re-planning is what makes it feedback.] [cite:@mayne2000constrained].@@html:</span>@@

fillstroke" d="M641.0,45.0L649.3,41.5L649.3,48.5Z"/></svg><figcaption>A plausible flight-control stack for the car, by analogy with published rocket-landing work. Only the attitude layer resembles the PID in this post. LQR is a linear-quadratic regulator and IMU an inertial measurement unit; the last paragraph of this section explains each layer.</figcaption></figure>

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p2" data-s="0">@@I tried this on the descent.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p2" data-s="1" data-ev>@@From the moment the car is upright again, 16.6 m up and falling at 8.8 m/s, the fuel-optimal descent needs 84 kg of nitrogen; the PID's sink-rate law, with the 1.1 g of braking fitted to the gauge, needs 127 kg on the same point-mass model.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p2" data-s="2" data-ev>@@The optimal profile holds a light 0.2 to 0.5 g while the car falls, then brakes near full thrust, 3.2 g, and arrives at touchdown speed at the ground.@@html:</span>@@ @@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p2" data-s="3" data-ev>@@That is closer to the real descent, which brakes at 3.3 g, than my PID is.@@html:</span>@@

@@html:<span class="zs" data-u="S14.p3" data-s="0" data-ev>@@The problem the guidance solves treats the car as a point with position @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x1D42B;</mi></mrow></math>@@ and velocity @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x1D42F;</mi></mrow></math>@@ in the vertical plane, pushed by a thrust @@html:<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>&#x1D42E;</mi></mrow></math>@@ per unit mass:@@html:</span>@@
